title: Planned vs Actual Crop Records and Lot Genealogy

content.overview: Plans change. Traceable cultivation records preserve what actually happened without erasing the original plan, allowing schedule accuracy, lot genealogy and recurring bottlenecks to be evaluated later.

vocabulary.definition: The intended timing recorded before an activity occurs.
The recorded timing when the activity truly occurred.
Difference between planned and actual timing, quantity or outcome.

sections.title: Keep planned and actual values separate
sections.body: Overwriting a plan with the actual date destroys information needed to understand schedule reliability.

sections.title: Crop identity should persist through stage changes
sections.body: Propagation batch, room assignment, harvest and post-harvest lot should be linked rather than recreated as unrelated records.

sections.title: Variance is improvement data
sections.body: Repeated delays in rooting, turnover or drying indicate capacity assumptions that should be adjusted in future plans.

workedExamples: A crop planned for transplant on June 1 but moved June 4 retains both dates and the reason rather than editing history.
When one veg batch is split into two flower rooms, both downstream lots retain the source relationship.
commonMistakes: Creating new IDs at every stage without genealogy.
Recording schedule variance but not reasons.
content.practicalApplication: For one crop, record planned and actual stage dates, room assignments, split/merge events, harvest lot and post-harvest destination, then calculate major variances.
content.summary: Planned-vs-actual records convert daily changes into traceable genealogy and better future capacity estimates.
